results.title: SageMaker Inference now supports Multi-Instance GPU to maximize GPU utilization for model endpoints | Artificial Intelligence
highlights:
# SageMaker Inference now supports Multi-Instance GPU to maximize GPU utilization for model endpoints

by Shantanu Tripathi, Apoorva Chandra, and Dmitry Soldatkin on 06 NOV 2026 in Amazon SageMaker AI, Announcements, Intermediate (200) Permalink Share

When you deploy a model to a GPU endpoint, the smallest unit of GPU you can request is one whole accelerator.

This constraint can cost you twice. First, you can’t host more models on an instance than it has accelerators. An `ml.p4d.24xlarge` has eight A100s, so it holds eight models, whether each one needs 40 GB or 14 GB. Second, and less obvious, it makes every deployment come down to a choice of which full GPU to deploy to. As your concurrency and prompt lengths grow, a full GPU on an older instance stops being enough, but a full GPU on a newer one is more than your model can use. You end up either under-served or paying for capability you never reach.

Today, Amazon SageMaker Inference supports GPU partitioning, which uses NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) to divide a physical GPU into independent partitions. Each partition receives a fixed share of the GPU’s compute units and a dedicated block of its memory, with isolation enforced in hardware. That changes both constraints: you can place a different model in each partition, and you can choose a fraction of a newer accelerator instead of a whole one of either generation.

...

Four things stand out.

- The partition is faster everywhere – It delivered more output tokens per second in every scenario at every concurrency, by 53 percent to 89 percent at the load where each scenario’s cost benefit is largest, and lower inter-token latency in every one too, by 8.9 percent to 42.1 percent. The gap widens with load.
- Time to first token is lower in every case, by 5.6 percent to 47.5 percent.
- On cost it’s 18–34 percent cheaper per million output tokens, above a crossover that moves earlier as prompts lengthen. Concurrency 64 for 100-token prompts, 4 for 8,000-token prompts. Below the crossover the whole A100 is the cheaper unit. These prices are all on-demand, which at the time of analysis were measured as $25.251286 per hour for an `ml.p4d.24xlarge` and $63.296000 per hour for an `ml.p5.48xlarge` in the US West (Oregon) AWS Region. Purely for our own analysis, we derived the unit cost by dividing the whole-instance cost by the number of units on it: 8 on the p4d, and 16 on the p5, where our partition is half of a GPU.
- At the top of the ladder on long-context traffic, the A100 stopped serving. On both the 6,000- and 8,000-token workloads it failed a third to a half of its requests against a serving-path deadline, while the partition failed none. That is why those two panels end earlier than the rest.

Treat this as a case-by-case comparison, not a verdict. The useful mental model is to regard the available GPU fractions as GPU types in their own right. List them alongside whole accelerators, work out what your traffic actually demands of compute and of memory, and compare them on your own workload. For high-concurrency, long-input traffic the partition won on both performance and cost here. For short-input or low-concurrency workloads the whole A100 remained cheaper. Partitioning isn’t a one-size-fits-all answer. It gives you more sizes to choose from, so you can pick the one that fits your workload.

...

Partitioning applies to real-time inference on inference component endpoints. Serverless endpoints and heterogeneous instance pools aren’t supported, and asynchronous invocation cannot address an inference component, so async workloads are out of scope.

You’re billed for the full GPU instance, as you are today. Partitioning raises how much of that instance you can use. It doesn’t change its hourly price.

Finally, a model that genuinely needs a full accelerator, or more than one, should keep having one. No partition spans accelerators.

...

It’s available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Europe (Frankfurt), and Europe (Ireland).

results.author: Amazon Web Services

# Amazon EMR on EKS reduces EMR charge by 30 percent

 Posted on: Oct 23, 2026 

Amazon EMR announces a reduction of 30 percent in the EMR charge added to EKS when running EMR on EKS. This price decrease applies to both the per-vCPU-hour charge and the per-GB-hour charge, while the underlying Amazon EKS charges remain unchanged. All EMR workloads running on the EKS deployment option benefit from this change. Now, you can run Apache Spark workloads on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) at a lower cost, and the new price automatically applies to your EMR on EKS workloads with no additional action required on your end.

The 30% reduction in EMR on EKS pricing is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon EMR on EKS is available. To learn more about EMR on EKS, visit the Amazon EMR on EKS documentation and the Amazon EMR pricing page.

results.title: Decoding quantum errors with NVIDIA Ising Decoding on AWS | AWS Quantum Technologies Blog
highlights:
Decoding quantum errors with NVIDIA Ising Decoding on AWS | AWS Quantum Technologies Blog

# Decoding quantum errors with NVIDIA Ising Decoding on AWS

by Benchen Huang, Almog Reshef, Linsey Rodenbach, Ishaan Pakrasi, and Tyler Takeshita on 21 OCT 2026 in Amazon Braket, Partner solutions, Quantum Technologies, Technical How-to Permalink Share

...

In this post we show how we trained NVIDIA Ising Decoding on AWS, how a range of accelerated compute instances compare in terms of performance and pricing, and how you can get started running similar workloads yourself.

...

AWS offers a broad and flexible range of accelerated compute instances, which makes it well suited for training machine learning (ML) models for QEC decoding. For this work we used Amazon EC2 P4d, P5, P5en, and P6 instances, accelerated by NVIDIA A100, H100, H200, and Blackwell B200 GPUs respectively, as well as G6e instances, accelerated by NVIDIA L40S GPUs. Every instance in this comparison provides eight GPUs, letting the pre-decoder train in a data-parallel fashion across all eight accelerators.

...

Ordered by GPU generation, the instances train progressively faster, cutting the average epoch time by up to about 39% from the A100-based P4d to the B200-based P6. The improvement is uneven and flattens at the top, where P5en and P6 finish within about 1 to 2% of each other, and the L40S in G6e keeps pace with the H100 in P5 to within about 6%. Based on Amazon EC2 On-Demand pricing in the US East (N. Virginia) Region as of October 2026, G6e is about 45% cheaper per hour than P5 while only about 6% slower, and P5en is about 44% cheaper per hour than P6 while only 1 to 2% slower. This lets you match the instance to the stage of the work, using G6e for high-volume early exploration and hyperparameter sweeps, and P5en or P6 when you want a trained model sooner or need the extra GPU memory for larger code distances. Ultimately, the most suitable instance depends on how you weight training time against budget for your workload.

...

Quantum error correction depends on decoders that are both accurate and fast enough to keep up with a quantum processor, and pre-decoding is one promising way to speed up the decoding pipeline. In this post we trained Ising Decoding on AWS across five accelerated compute instance types, spanning four NVIDIA GPU generations, using a single containerized workflow on AWS PCS. We found that each newer GPU generation delivers faster training, and that cost varies just as much across instances, so the right instance depends on the stage of your work and your budget. We also validated the trained pre-decoder on AWS, where it reduced decoding latency at large code distances while improving the logical error rate. To get started, you can find the code in the NVIDIA Ising Decoding GitHub repository, and an AWS sample for PCS setup. Together they let you reproduce these benchmarks and adapt the workflow to your own QEC models.

# AWS launches support for amortization of EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML

 Posted on: Nov 6, 2026 

AWS Data Exports for Cost and Usage Report (CUR) 2.0 and AWS Cost Explorer now amortize the upfront fee for Amazon EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML across the duration of each reservation. You can see the amortized cost of each instance launched into a Capacity Block and the amortized cost of unused capacity, so you can attribute your upfront fee to the workloads that used it and identify capacity that went unused.

Previously, a Capacity Block's upfront fee appeared as a single charge on the purchase date, making it difficult to see how that cost was spread across usage over the reservation. Now the amortized cost appears alongside your instance usage, so you can allocate GPU costs to the teams, projects, and applications that ran on the reserved capacity. You can also see what share of your reservation went unused and plan future Capacity Block purchases. In CUR 2.0, the amortized costs appear in the reservation_amortized_upfront_fee_for_billing_period, reservation_effective_cost columns, and reservation_net_effective_cost shows the amortized cost after discounts. In Cost Explorer, select the amortized cost view to see Capacity Block costs allocated for the reservation.

 Amortization for Capacity Blocks is available at no additional charge in all AWS Regions except the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions and the China Regions. To learn more, see the CUR 2.0 data dictionary and exploring your data using Cost Explorer.

Posted on: Nov 6, 2026 

Starting today, you can add Amazon EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML and interruptible Capacity Reservations to Capacity Reservation Resource Groups in AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. Amazon EC2 offers different reservation offerings such as On-Demand Capacity Reservations (ODCRs), interruptible Capacity Reservations, and Capacity Blocks for ML. Previously, a Capacity Reservation Resource Group could only include ODCRs. Now you can add any type of Capacity Reservation to a Capacity Reservation Resource Group, making it easier to launch EC2 instances across your entire portfolio of reserved capacity.

...

With the addition of AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, this feature is now available in all AWS Regions where Capacity Blocks for ML and interruptible ODCRs are supported, excluding China Regions. To get started, see Capacity Reservation Resource Groups and the Capacity Reservations user guide.

# Amazon EC2 G7 instances now available in Europe (Frankfurt) and Europe (Stockholm) Regions

 Posted on: Oct 12, 2026 

Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) G7 instances powered by NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs are now available in Europe (Frankfurt) and Europe (Stockholm) Regions. G7 instances deliver up to 4.6x AI inference performance and up to 2.1 graphics performance compared to G6 instances. G7 instances also deliver faster performance for GPU-accelerated data analytics workloads.

Customers can use G7 instances for deploying AI models for language translation, video and image analysis, speech recognition and recommender systems. They also accelerate graphics workloads such as creating and rendering real-time, cinematic-quality graphics and game streaming. Additionally, G7 instances support video transcoding, spatial computing, and data analytics workloads. G7 instances feature up to 8 NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs with 32 GB of memory per GPU and custom Intel Xeon 6 processors. They support up to 192 virtual CPUs (vCPUs) and up to 700 Gbps of Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) networking bandwidth. They also support up to 768 GiB of system memory, and up to 7.6 TB of local NVMe SSD storage.

You can use G7 instances for Amazon EC2 in the following AWS Regions: US West (Oregon), US East (N. Virginia, Ohio) and Europe (Spain, Frankfurt, Stockholm). You can purchase G7 instances as On-Demand Instances, Spot Instances, or as part of Savings Plans.

results.author: Amazon Web Services
highlights:
# Announcing consumption-based pricing for short-term memory in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

 Posted on: Oct 12, 2026 

Announcing consumption-based pricing for short-term memory in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory now prices short-term memory (STM) based on the data your agents ingest, retrieve, and store, replacing the previous flat rate per event. AgentCore memory gives agents in-session context through short-term memory and persistent knowledge across sessions through long-term memory. With consumption-based pricing, developers building agents that write frequent, small events pay in proportion to what they use.

STM is priced across three dimensions: ingestion at $1.00 per GB, retrieval at $0.20 per GB, and storage at $0.10 per GB-month. Ingestion and retrieval are billed per event with a 12 KB minimum and 64 KB maximum billable size, while storage is billed on each event's actual size. Most workloads see lower costs, with small-payload use cases seeing the largest reductions. You can manage storage costs by setting a shorter time to live (TTL) on your memory resources. Long-term memory pricing is unchanged.

Consumption-based pricing for AgentCore Memory short-term memory is available in all AWS Regions where AgentCore Memory is offered. To get started, visit the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore pricing page.

results.author: Amazon Web Services
highlights:
# Amazon ECS now supports GPU sharing with NVIDIA Multi-Process Service (MPS)

 Posted on: Oct 27, 2026 

Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) now supports GPU sharing with NVIDIA Multi-Process Service (MPS), enabling you to run multiple Amazon ECS tasks concurrently on a single NVIDIA GPU. GPU sharing helps you increase GPU utilization and reduce infrastructure costs for workloads that use only part of a GPU's capacity, such as small-model inference, AV/ADAS simulations, embedding generation, and multi-model serving.

With GPU sharing, you can pack more workloads onto each GPU instance without changing your application code. You define the GPU memory each container needs and can optionally set a maximum share of GPU compute, and Amazon ECS places tasks on GPUs with available capacity as your services scale and deploy. GPU sharing is supported on Amazon ECS Managed Instances and Amazon ECS on Amazon EC2. On Amazon ECS Managed Instances, Amazon ECS also monitors the MPS control daemon that enables sharing on each instance. If the daemon stops or becomes unhealthy, Amazon ECS automatically replaces the instance and moves your tasks to healthy capacity, so your GPU workloads keep running without manual intervention.

results.author: Amazon Web Services
highlights:
# Amazon EC2 Hpc8a instances are now available in Asia Pacific (Singapore)

 Posted on: Oct 5, 2026 

Starting today, Amazon EC2 Hpc8a instances are available in Asia Pacific (Singapore) region. These instances are powered by 5th Gen AMD EPYC processors (formerly code named Turin). With a maximum frequency of 4.5GHz, Hpc8a instances deliver up to 40% higher performance and up to 25% better price performance compared to Hpc7a instances, helping customers accelerate compute-intensive workloads while optimizing costs. Compared to Hpc7a instances, Hpc8a instances also provide up to 42% higher memory bandwidth, further improving performance for memory-intensive simulations and scientific computing workloads. Built on the latest sixth-generation AWS Nitro Cards, Hpc8a instances are designed for compute-intensive, latency-sensitive HPC workloads. They are ideal for tightly coupled applications such as computational fluid dynamics (CFD), weather forecasting, explicit finite element analysis (FEA), and multiphysics simulations that require fast inter-node communication and consistent high performance. To get started, sign in to the AWS Management Console. For more information visit the Amazon EC2 Hpc8a instance page or AWS news blog.
